vignette:
He is a 62-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life working in high-risk environments, and he speaks about danger with the weary familiarity of someone who has learned to manage fear by narrowing his attention. For years, he works as a bomb disposal technician, a job that asks him to move carefully toward objects everyone else runs from. He takes pride in that work, in being the one people call when a situation has become too dangerous to approach. He is married, and his wife has long known how he steadies himself before leaving home, checking and rechecking his gear in quiet ritual, then pausing a moment at the door as if preparing both body and mind for what the day may demand.

The traumatic event that changes him comes during an operation involving a suspected explosive device contaminated with toxic chemicals. He remembers the scene in fragments: the sealed suit, the metallic smell, the tension in his shoulders, the ordinary concentration he brings to difficult tasks. Then there is a failure in containment, an unexpected release, and the sharp realization that something invisible has entered the air around him. He feels the first sting in his eyes and throat before he understands the seriousness of it. Even now, he describes that moment not as loud or dramatic, but as deeply violating-his body suddenly no longer trustworthy, the air itself turned against him. He is evacuated, treated, and survives, but the event lodges in him in a way that is hard to explain to others because there is no single image that contains it. It is the sensation of exposure, of being trapped inside danger that cannot be seen.

In the weeks afterward, he expects the fear to settle once his body recovers, but instead his mind keeps returning to the scene. He finds himself replaying the sequence in his head while driving, while shaving, while lying awake beside his wife. He wakes in the night with his chest tight and his mouth dry, certain for a few seconds that he smells chemicals again. At work, he becomes more cautious in ways that are useful and more guarded in ways that distress him. He begins checking equipment repeatedly, then checking the checks. He notices how his attention has narrowed to exits, ventilation, sealed containers, the behavior of his own breathing. He tells himself this is professionalism, but privately he knows he is straining. He is no longer simply assessing risk; he is bracing for catastrophe.

He starts avoiding anything that reminds him of the exposure. He leaves the television off when news reports mention industrial accidents or emergency responses. He asks his wife to handle certain cleaning products because their odor makes his stomach clench. On some mornings, he stands in the garage with the door open longer than necessary, needing fresh air before he can enter the house. His wife notices that he becomes quiet and distant after deployments or training exercises. He loves her company but finds himself less able to relax into conversation, as though part of him remains on watch even at home. He is ashamed by how easily ordinary things now irritate him: a sudden noise, a strong smell, someone standing too close behind him. He reacts fast, sometimes with anger that arrives before thought, and afterward he feels embarrassed and exhausted.

The most painful change for him is the loss of ease in his own body. He used to trust his physical discipline, trust that he could perform under pressure. Now he is more aware of fatigue, of headaches, of a tightness in his chest that sends him immediately back to the day of the exposure. When he feels his heartbeat quicken, he wonders whether he is having a medical problem or simply remembering one. His nights are often broken by shallow sleep and vivid dreams in which he is again unable to breathe properly, again trying to leave a contaminated space but not reaching it in time. In the morning, he rises tired and already on edge, carrying the day as if it starts in the middle of something unfinished.

Still, he keeps working, partly because he does not want the event to define him, and partly because he does not yet know how to be anyone else. He moves through his routines with discipline, though there is now a vigilance in him that feels less like strength than strain. He watches himself watching the world. At 62, after a lifetime of facing explosive threats, he is unsettled by how a toxic substance-unseen, odorless at first, everywhere and nowhere-has changed his relationship to safety, sleep, and trust.
